# The Gateway Layer: Routing, Cost, and Governance {#sec-gateway}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Two small measurements, both seconds of compute:
fifteen labelled query pairs through `nomic-embed-text` to ask whether one
similarity threshold can separate a cache hit from a bug, and a follow-up that
investigates a defect in that embedder which the first measurement exposed.
The routing and reliability material is cited rather than measured — a retry
storm is not something to reproduce on a laptop, and the routing argument rests
on published cascades plus a signal measurement this book already made in
@sec-classification. Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `nomic-embed-text`, on
Python 3.14.5, Apple Silicon.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- name the specific problems a model gateway removes, and say when you do not
  have them yet;
- enforce budgets and quotas knowing which half of a request's cost you can
  price in advance and which half you cannot;
- design failover across providers without building the retry storm that turns
  a degradation into an outage;
- judge a cost-routing proposal by the signal it depends on rather than by the
  architecture;
- treat exact-match and semantic response caching as different features with
  different risks;
- pin model versions and migrate off deprecated ones behind an eval gate.

## What a gateway is for {#sec-gateway-why}

@sec-serving was about one request against one model. A gateway is what appears
when there is more than one of either: a single service that every LLM call in
the organisation passes through, presenting one API and hiding which provider
answers.

It is worth being precise about *when* that becomes worth building, because a
gateway is infrastructure and infrastructure has a standing cost. The problems
it removes do not exist on day one:

| the problem | when it shows up |
|:--|:--|
| Provider keys are pasted into several services, and rotating one means finding them all | the second service |
| Nobody can say which team spent what | the second team |
| A runaway loop bills for six hours before anyone notices | the first agent |
| Switching provider means editing every caller | the second provider |
| A model is deprecated and you cannot enumerate who calls it | the first deprecation |
| Policy — redaction, residency, audit — is implemented three times, differently | the first audit |

: Six problems, and the moment each one arrives {tbl-colwidths="[62,38]"}

[Every one of those is an *attribution* problem or a *choke point* problem, and
both are solved by having exactly one place the traffic passes through.]{.hl}
That is the whole argument. A gateway does not make any single request better —
@sec-serving is where request-level performance lives — it makes the
*population* of requests governable.

The corresponding anti-pattern is building one before the second team exists,
which adds a network hop (one more server between caller and provider), a
failure mode and an on-call rotation (someone who must fix it at night) in
exchange for problems you do not have.

## Budgets, quotas, and the half you cannot price in advance {#sec-gateway-budgets}

Attribution is the first thing the choke point buys, and the moment you can
attribute spend somebody will ask you to limit it. That is where the
architecture stops being free.

The usual gateway control is a **virtual key**: a per-team, per-service or
per-feature credential that maps to the real provider key and carries limits of
its own. Because callers never hold the real key, a leaked virtual key can be
revoked on its own, and the provider key is rotated in one place. Three limits,
routinely confused, failing differently:

| control | what it bounds | what happens at the limit |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Rate limit** | requests or tokens per second or minute | requests are shed or queued; recovers on its own |
| **Quota** | requests or tokens per period | the caller is blocked until the period rolls over |
| **Budget** | money per period | [the interesting one]{.hl} |

: Three limits that are not the same thing {tbl-colwidths="[18,38,44]"}

Rate limits are usually built as a **token bucket** — and here "token" means a
permit, not an LLM token. A bucket holds at most $B$ permits and refills at a
steady $r$ permits per second; each request takes one (or, for a token-per-minute
limit, as many as it has LLM tokens), and a request that finds the bucket empty
is refused, typically with HTTP status 429 and a `Retry-After` header saying
when to come back. A full bucket lets a burst of $B$ requests through at once,
while over any long period the average cannot exceed $r$. Providers enforce
their own limits in requests and tokens per minute, so set the gateway's limits
below the provider's: then the gateway, not the provider, decides whose traffic
is shed.

Budgets are the interesting one because of an asymmetry that comes straight out
of @sec-serving's two halves. **You know the input tokens before the request
runs and the output tokens only after.** Prefill is countable in advance — the
prompt is right there — but decode produces an unknown number of tokens, and on
most providers output is the dearer half per token.

So a pre-request budget check is necessarily approximate, and there are three
honest ways to handle that:

**Reserve the maximum.** Price the request as if it will generate `max_tokens`,
check that against the remaining budget, reconcile down afterwards. Safe, and it
under-serves: a budget with room for one maximal request refuses ten small ones.

**Admit optimistically and reconcile.** Charge input cost plus an estimate,
settle the real number on completion. This is what most gateways do, and it
means a budget can be exceeded by roughly one request's worth of output per
concurrent caller. Usually fine — but state it, so nobody is surprised.

**Cap the output.** Set `max_tokens` per virtual key. It does not make the cost
*known* — a request can stop anywhere below the cap — but it bounds it, which is
what makes the first option cheap: a reservation against a known ceiling is a
reservation you can actually afford to make. This is the one teams skip. Two
things fall outside the cap: every retry is a new request billed again, and
per-call tool fees (a hosted web search, say) are priced separately. Reasoning
tokens are billed as output; check that your provider counts them inside the
cap, since the parameter's name and scope differ between APIs.

One implementation detail decides whether any of this holds under load. The
check and the reservation must be **atomic** — a Lua script on Redis, a
`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, a conditional write — because read-then-write across $c$
concurrent callers lets all $c$ of them see the same remaining budget and all
of them pass, even when the budget had room for only one. The overshoot then
grows with the number of concurrent callers — with your traffic, exactly when
you least want it to.

The same log that enforces the budget is the cost tracker: the gateway turns
each call's token counts into money with a per-model price table (uncached
input, cached input, output — the three prices of @sec-serving's worksheet).
Keep that table versioned, because prices change and a stale one makes every
report quietly wrong.

::: {.column-margin}
The same asymmetry decides what a cost dashboard can *do*. Input cost is
knowable at admission and can therefore be enforced; output cost is observable
only at completion and can only be reported. Any control that must *stop*
something has to act on the input side or on a cap — which is why `max_tokens`
is a budget control and not only a quality one.
:::

Whether the ceiling is hard is a product decision, not an engineering one. A
hard ceiling stops the spend and stops the feature; an alert preserves the
feature and does not stop the spend. A workable default is a hard ceiling on
*non-production* keys, where a runaway loop is the likeliest cause, and alerting
with a much higher ceiling on production, where the likeliest cause is success.

## Failover, and the retry that made it worse {#sec-gateway-failover}

Multi-provider failover is why many teams adopt a gateway, and it is where a
gateway most easily makes an incident worse instead of better.

The mechanism is well documented outside this field. When a provider degrades,
every client sees slow or failing requests and retries. Those retries arrive
exactly when the provider has least spare capacity, so more requests fail, so
more clients retry. Google's SRE book treats this as a cascading failure, and the
remedies it describes generalise directly [@beyer2016sre].

Three controls, and a gateway is the natural home for all three because it is
the only component that sees the whole population:

- **Exponential backoff with jitter.** *Backoff* means waiting longer after
  each failed attempt; *exponential* means the wait doubles; *jitter* means the
  wait is randomised. A common recipe ("full jitter") waits a random time
  between 0 and $\min(\text{cap},\ \text{base} \cdot 2^n)$ before retry $n$.
  Backoff alone keeps clients that failed together retrying together; the
  jitter is what spreads them out. Clients retrying at exactly 1s, 2s, 4s
  reproduce the thundering herd — many clients hitting the provider in the
  same instant — at every step.
- **A circuit breaker.** After a threshold of failures, stop sending to that
  provider for a cooling period rather than continuing to spend latency
  rediscovering that it is still down. The breaker is *closed* (traffic flows)
  in normal operation, *open* (traffic goes to the fallback or fails at once)
  after the threshold, and *half-open* after the cooling period, when a few
  trial requests decide whether it closes again.
- **A retry budget.** Google runs two [@beyer2016sre], and the second is the one
  people skip: a
  per-request cap of three attempts, *and* a per-client cap where each client
  tracks the share of its requests that are retries and stops retrying once that
  ratio passes 10%. The per-request cap alone still lets the load approach 3×
  when nearly everything fails, which is exactly when the provider can least
  absorb it; the fraction brings the worst case down to about 1.1×.

Two practical rules sit underneath all three. **Retry only what can succeed on
a second try**: 429s, 5xx server errors and timeouts, honouring any
`Retry-After` — not a 400 for a malformed request or a prompt longer than the
context window, which will fail identically every time. And **retry at one
layer only**. Provider SDKs already retry by default (the OpenAI and Anthropic
Python clients make two retries), so an SDK, a gateway and an application each
allowing three attempts can turn one request into $3^3 = 27$ attempts; the SRE book calls
this a combinatorial explosion [@beyer2016sre]. Timeouts need the same care: an
LLM response can legitimately take a minute, so a single short total timeout
cuts off long answers, while a generous one hides a hung provider. With
streaming, time out on the wait for the first token and, separately, on the
gap between tokens.

There is also a failure mode specific to LLM gateways, and it is not a
reliability problem at all:

[A failover changes the model, and a different model gives different
answers.]{.hl} Falling back from one provider's flagship to another's is not
like failing over between replicas of a database. Output format drifts,
tool-calling syntax differs, refusal behaviour differs, and a structured-output
parser tuned on one may reject the other's output entirely (@sec-decoding).

Which makes failover an evaluation question. The honest options are to evaluate
the fallback path on the same suite as the primary — @sec-production-eval is
where that belongs — or to fail *closed* with a clear error rather than silently
serving output from a model nobody tested. Failing closed is frequently right
and rarely the default.

## Routing by cost, and the signal it depends on {#sec-gateway-routing}

The idea is irresistible: most requests are easy, easy requests do not need the
expensive model, so send those to a cheap one and escalate the rest. Done well
this is the largest cost lever a gateway has. Done by assertion it quietly
degrades quality on exactly the requests nobody sampled.

Two shapes, and they fail differently:

| | how it decides | what it needs |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Cascade** | run the cheap model, escalate if the answer looks unreliable | a signal computed *after* the cheap call — so you pay for it |
| **Router** | classify the request first, send it to one model | a signal computed *before* any call — cheaper, and harder |

: Two ways to route, and what each one costs {tbl-colwidths="[16,44,40]"}

The published results are encouraging. FrugalGPT cascades over a set of APIs and
reports matching the best individual model's accuracy at a small fraction of that
model's cost, or improving accuracy at equal cost [@chen2023frugalgpt]. RouteLLM learns
a router from preference data and reports large cost reductions while retaining
most of the strong model's quality on the benchmarks it was evaluated on
[@ong2024routellm].

[But every one of those results is a claim about a *signal*, and the signal is
where routing succeeds or fails.]{.hl} The architecture is trivial; knowing
which requests are the hard ones is the entire problem.

This book has already measured the most tempting signal and found it wanting.
@sec-classification asked a model to state its own confidence in words and then
tested that confidence as a detector of its own errors: **AUROC 0.667, against
0.843 for a proper probability**. It is better than nothing — the mean
confidence really is higher on correct answers — and it is a long way from the
instrument a routing policy needs.

A cascade built on it escalates many easy requests and misses many hard ones,
and both mistakes are invisible in an aggregate accuracy number.

Which produces the rule that matters more than any routing framework:

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Report the random-escalation baseline.** For any routing policy, compute what
you would get by escalating the same *fraction* of requests chosen at random.
If your clever signal does not beat that curve, it is not a signal — you are
buying accuracy with escalation rate alone, and a coin flip would do it more
cheaply.

This is the same control discipline as @sec-summarization's copied-text check
and @sec-agent-eval's outcome-versus-trajectory split: a measurement without a
baseline that should fail cannot tell you anything.
:::

Three practical notes, none of which need a paper:

**An escalated request pays for both calls.** It costs small-model tokens
*plus* large-model tokens, so a cascade that escalates a fraction $e$ of traffic
costs $C_{\text{small}} + e \cdot C_{\text{large}}$ against $C_{\text{large}}$
for sending everything to the big model. At $e = 0.5$ and a 10× price ratio that
is $0.1 + 0.5 = 0.6$ of the large model's bill — a real saving, and nothing like
half. Compute the break-even rate before building it, with your price ratio
rather than the benchmark's: the cascade saves money only while
$e < 1 - C_{\text{small}}/C_{\text{large}}$, which is $0.9$ at a 10× ratio and
$0.5$ at a 2× ratio.

**Routing changes the model, so it inherits every problem from
@sec-gateway-failover.** Different output format, different tool-call syntax,
different refusal behaviour. A router is a deliberate, permanent version of the
thing failover does by accident.

**Capability routing is easier than quality routing.** "This request needs
vision", "this one needs a 200k-token context window", "this one must stay in the EU" are
properties you can read off the request without predicting anything. They are
also the routing rules most likely to survive contact with production, because
they do not depend on a signal that might be AUROC 0.667.

## Two kinds of cache, and only one is safe {#sec-gateway-cache}

Response caching at the gateway is a different mechanism from @sec-serving's
prompt caching: that one reuses a *prefix's* KV cache inside the server, this
one returns a stored answer and never calls the model at all.

**Exact-match caching** keys on `(model, full prompt, parameters)` and returns a
byte-identical previous response. Its quality risk is not zero — it is
*controllable*, which is a different claim: the identical prompt is the right
answer only while everything the answer depended on and the key did not capture
has stayed the same. That list is longer than it looks. The model *version*, not
just the alias, or a silent provider upgrade serves yesterday's model. The
decoding parameters, or a temperature change serves stale output. The tenant
(the customer organisation whose data this is) and the caller's permissions,
or you serve one customer's answer to another. Any tool result or retrieved
document the answer was built from. And time itself, which is what a TTL
(*time to live*: how long an entry may be served before it expires) is for —
*what is our refund policy* has a shelf life even
when nothing else changes. Get the key and the TTL right and the risk really is
gone; get them wrong and it is invisible, because a stale hit looks exactly like
a correct one.

**Semantic caching** embeds the request and returns a stored answer when some
previous request is *similar enough*. Same word, different feature, and the
difference is that this one can be wrong.

[A semantic cache is an approximate nearest-neighbour search whose false
positives are answers to questions nobody asked.]{.hl} Fifteen pairs of support
queries, labelled by what a cache *should* do, embedded with
`nomic-embed-text` and sorted by cosine similarity:

```text
   sim   hit?   pair
 0.982  False   is the pump covered by the warranty?    | is the pump not covered by the warranty?
 0.957  False   should i upgrade to the pro plan?       | should i avoid upgrading to the pro plan?
 0.957  False   ship 200 units to ankara                | ship 500 units to ankara
 0.954   True   how much does the pro plan cost?        | what is the price of the pro plan?
 0.917  False   what was revenue in q1 2025?            | what was revenue in q1 2026?
 0.913   True   can i get a refund?                     | is a refund possible?
 0.907  False   can i use this outdoors?                | can i not use this outdoors?
 0.898   True   how do i cancel my subscription?        | how can i end my subscription?
 0.891  False   cancel order 4471                       | cancel order 4417
 0.856   True   how do i reset my password?             | i forgot my password, how can i change it?
 0.851  False   what are your business hours on monday? | what are your business hours on sunday?
 0.742  False   what is the price of the pro plan?      | what is the price of the basic plan?
 0.712  False   how do i reset my password?             | how do i reset my api key?
 0.703  False   how do i export my data?                | how do i delete my data?
 0.609   True   what are your business hours?           | when are you open?
```

Read the top of that list. [The single most similar pair in the whole set is a
sentence and its negation]{.hl} — 0.982 — and the second and third are a
negation and a changed quantity. Meanwhile the genuinely identical question,
*what are your business hours* against *when are you open*, sits at the very
bottom on 0.609.

The consequence is arithmetic rather than opinion. The lowest true pair is
0.609 and the highest false pair is 0.982, so the two classes' ranges interleave
and **no single threshold separates them on this set**.

The two error types are not interchangeable, so sweep the thresholds with that
in mind. A *miss* costs a model call and the user never knows. A *false hit*
costs a wrong answer, served confidently, with nothing logged. Across every cut
on this set the fewest total errors — five — belongs to the degenerate
threshold that caches nothing at all, and all five of those are misses. The
best cut that actually serves anything sits at 0.982 and returns exactly one
cache hit: the sentence and its negation. **On this sample, the one hit the best
serving cut earned you was wrong, and any cut loose enough to catch a genuine
paraphrase also served at least three wrong answers.**

Read as a detector, cosine similarity scores an **AUROC of 0.44** here — below
the 0.5 a coin flip would give. Five positives against ten negatives puts an
enormous interval on that, so the honest reading is not "similarity is
anti-correlated with sameness". It is that fifteen pairs cannot find you a
threshold, and they can tell you the search will not be easy.

This is the sentence-level cousin of @sec-embeddings' antonym result, where
`increase`/`decrease` scored **0.881** — level with `cat`/`dog` at 0.880. At
the sentence level it gets worse rather than better: negation adds one short
token among many, and pooling — averaging the token vectors into one sentence
vector — averages it away, so *is covered* and *is
not covered* land nearly on top of one another. They are related, which is what
the model was trained to capture. They are also opposite, and a cache cannot
tell.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The instrument had a defect, and finding it is the lesson.** The table above
is lowercased, and it did not start that way. Written naturally, *business hours
on Monday* and *business hours on Sunday* came back at cosine **1.000** — not
close, *byte-identical vectors*.

Following that produced a reproducible finding about the tool rather than about
caching. With `nomic-embed-text` served by `ollama` 0.24.0, any capitalised word
collapses to one constant token:

```text
"Monday" == "Cat" == "Ankara" == "Paris" == "Toyota" == "XYZZY" == "Q"
  -> all byte-identical vectors

"Cat sat on the mat" == "Dog sat on the mat"     identical
"cat sat on the mat" vs "dog sat on the mat"     cos 0.879, different
"Monday" vs "monday"                             cos 0.486
```

All 21 pairs of weekday names are identical to each other; so are January and
February, and Ankara and Istanbul. Lowercase text behaves normally. It
reproduces on both `/api/embed` and `/api/embeddings`.

**What this is and is not.** It is one machine's reproducible observation, and
three things a defect report would need are missing from it. The model was
pulled by its floating tag rather than by digest, which is the exact failure
@sec-gateway-versions is about, arriving in this chapter's own instrument. The
same weights were not run through a second stack — `sentence-transformers` on
the original checkpoint — so the fault has not been isolated to the GGUF
conversion, the tokenizer or the server. And `nomic-embed-text` expects a task
prefix (`search_query: `, `search_document: `), which was not used; whether the
collapse survives one is untested, and since prefixes are lowercase it is a
plausible interaction rather than an idle question. Treat it as an observation,
not a characterised defect, and pin a digest before you report one.

Two things make it more than a curiosity. A likely mechanism, untested here:
this model uses a lowercase-only (BERT-style "uncased") vocabulary, so if the
serving stack skips the lowercasing step, every capitalised word falls outside
the vocabulary and becomes the same unknown-word token. And the same symptom has
been reported upstream as
[ollama issue #13942](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13942), "nomic-embed-text
embedding incorrect for uppercase" — a regression reported from 0.13.1 and fixed
in the 0.30 series, a range that includes the 0.24.0 used here. The fix changes
the vectors, which is the other half of the lesson: an embedder or server
upgrade silently invalidates every vector a semantic cache has stored.

None of that changes what the chapter takes from it, because [a semantic cache
built on that embedder would have served Monday's answer to Sunday's question,
at similarity 1.000, every time, with nothing in any log.]{.hl}

It is the same shape as @sec-summarization's `rouge-score` tokenizer and
@sec-text-as-data's Turkish lowercasing: the tool did not fail, it returned
plausible numbers. The only reason it surfaced is that a pair which *had* to
score low scored highest.
:::

So treat the two caches as different features with different bars:

| | quality risk | where it belongs |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Exact-match | [controllable — none once the key and TTL capture everything the answer depended on]{.pro} | on by default, wherever a repeated answer is acceptable (not where users ask to regenerate a sampled answer) |
| Semantic | [a wrong answer, silently]{.con} | only with a measured false-positive rate on your own traffic, and never on anything consequential |

: Two caches that share a name {tbl-colwidths="[18,38,44]"}

And note that accuracy is not the only axis a semantic cache moves. It is also
a store of prompts and answers sitting inside the one component every request
passes through, which makes three things the gateway's problem rather than
somebody else's. The first two apply to the exact-match cache too — it stores
prompts and it can cross tenants just as easily; only the third is specific to
similarity:

- **Key by tenant, and by user where the data is personal.** A cache keyed on
  the embedding alone will serve one customer's answer to another customer's
  question. That is not a quality defect, it is a data leak, and it looks
  exactly like a cache hit in every metric you have.
- **The retention rule applies to the cache.** Cache entries hold the prompt.
  A policy that says you do not log prompts is untrue the moment a semantic
  cache stores them, so give the cache the same TTL and the same redaction as
  @sec-gateway-policy gives the log.
- **Decide what invalidates an entry.** A price changes, a policy is updated,
  a document is retracted — and a cached answer keeps being served with no
  version attached to it. If you cannot name the event that clears an entry,
  the entry is permanent. Upgrading the embedding model or its server is one
  such event: stored vectors from the old version are no longer comparable
  with new ones.

If you do build one, the measurement that makes it defensible is the one nobody
runs: sample the cache *hits*, check by hand how many were genuinely the same
question, and report that rate with an interval (@sec-data-annotation). A hit
rate without a correctness rate is a number that only looks like evidence. And
before any of that, embed two inputs you know must differ and confirm the
embedder can tell them apart.

## Pinning versions, and surviving a deprecation {#sec-gateway-versions}

An LLM behind a stable name is not a stable dependency. Providers update the
model an unversioned alias points at, and the failure that follows has a
distinctive shape: nothing errors, nothing is logged, and your outputs change.

[A silent model upgrade is a dependency change that bypasses every gate you
have.]{.hl} It appears in no diff, triggers no test run, and arrives on the
provider's schedule rather than yours.

The gateway is where this is fixed, in three parts:

**Callers ask for an alias; the gateway resolves it to a pinned version.**
Application code says `summarizer`, the gateway maps that to a dated model
identifier. One edit changes what every caller gets, and — more usefully — one
query answers "who is still on the old model?"

**Migration runs behind an eval gate.** Point the alias at the new version for a
small share of traffic, score both on the suite from @sec-production-eval, and
promote only if it holds. This is ordinary dependency-upgrade discipline; the
difference is that without a gateway there is nowhere to put the traffic split.

**Deprecations get a countdown you can act on.** Providers retire models with
notice, and the notice is useless if you cannot enumerate the callers. The
gateway's request log is that enumeration.

::: {.column-margin}
Worth pinning even when you never intend to migrate deliberately: an alias that
moves silently makes every historical evaluation unreproducible. A score from
three months ago is a score for a model you can no longer name, which quietly
undermines every regression comparison drawn from it.
:::

## One choke point for policy {#sec-gateway-policy}

The last argument for a gateway matters most to everybody outside engineering,
and it is structural rather than technical.

Redaction, audit logging, data residency and retention are all *cross-cutting*:
they must hold for every call, and a policy that holds for four services out of
five does not hold. Implementing them per service guarantees drift, because five
teams will make five slightly different decisions and only one of them will be
wrong in a way anybody notices.

| policy | what it needs | why it belongs at the gateway |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Redaction | strip or tokenize personal data before it leaves | one implementation, uniformly applied — @sec-guardrails has the mechanics |
| Audit | who called what model with what, and when | the gateway is the only component that sees every call |
| Residency | route EU data to EU endpoints | the routing half is a routing decision, and routing already lives here. It is only the half: the contract with the provider, where sub-processors sit, and where logs and caches land all have to agree, and an EU endpoint alone settles none of them |
| Retention | do not log prompts containing personal data, or log them briefly | one retention rule rather than five |

: Four policies and why one place beats five {tbl-colwidths="[16,40,44]"}

The obligations themselves — lawful basis, DPIA, the EU AI Act's tiers, KVKK's
requirements — are @sec-governance's subject. What belongs here is the
architectural claim they depend on: [a policy you cannot enforce in one place is
a policy you are hoping about.]{.hl}

There is a cost, and it should be stated plainly. A gateway sits on the critical
path of every LLM call in the organisation, so its availability is a ceiling on
everyone's availability and its latency is added to everyone's latency. That is
a real trade, and it is why the answer to "should we build one?" is "not yet"
until the problems in @sec-gateway-why actually exist.

## Intuition checks {#sec-gateway-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. The first two ask whether to build this
layer at all and what it can honestly promise once you have; the middle two are
the places a gateway most easily makes things worse, by amplifying an outage or
by dressing a coin flip up as a router; and the last two are the silent
failures — an answer served from a question nobody asked, and a model that
changed without a deploy.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. One team, one provider, one service. Do you need a gateway?

No, and building one now is a net loss.

Every problem a gateway solves is a problem of *plurality*: several callers to
attribute, several providers to abstract, several policies to keep identical.
With one of each you have none of them, and what you gain by adding the layer
is a network hop, a deployment, and a component whose availability is now a
ceiling on your own.

The honest trigger is the second of anything — the second team, the second
provider, or the first agent that can loop. Until then a client library and a
spending alert cover it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Can a gateway enforce an exact spending cap?

Not unless it caps output length.

Input tokens are countable before the call; output tokens are known only when
the call finishes, and output is usually the more expensive half. So admission
control is either pessimistic — reserve `max_tokens` worth of budget and
reconcile down, which refuses requests you could have afforded — or optimistic,
which can overshoot by roughly one request's worth of output per concurrent
caller.

Setting `max_tokens` per virtual key is what turns an unknown final cost into a
reservable upper bound — for the output it limits. Retries and per-call tool
fees sit outside it and need reserving too, and reasoning tokens only count if
your provider includes them in the cap.
It is the cheapest control in this chapter and the one most often left unset.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your provider is degraded and your gateway retries. What could go wrong?

You can convert a partial degradation into a full outage.

Retries arrive precisely when the provider has least spare capacity, so more
requests fail, so more clients retry. The controls are backoff *with jitter*,
because plain backoff re-synchronises the fleet into a herd; a circuit breaker,
so you stop spending latency to rediscover an outage; and a retry budget as a
*fraction* of traffic — Google's clients stop retrying once retries pass 10% of
their requests, on top of a three-attempt per-request cap.

The per-request cap is the one everybody implements, and on its own it still
lets the load approach 3× in the worst case — more if several layers each
retry. The fraction brings that down to about 1.1×.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your routing policy cut cost 40% and accuracy fell 1 point. Good trade?

Unanswerable until you see the random-escalation baseline.

Escalating *any* 40% of requests to the strong model buys some accuracy back,
signal or no signal. The question is whether your policy beats a coin flip at
the same escalation rate — and if it does not, you have not built a router, you
have built an expensive random number generator.

Run that baseline first. It costs nothing, since you already have both models'
answers on the evaluation set, and it is the only thing that separates a signal
from a rate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Semantic caching gets a 30% hit rate. Ship it?

Not on that number alone, because it does not contain the thing that matters.

A hit rate says how often the cache answered. It says nothing about how often
it answered *correctly*, and a semantic cache's failure mode is returning a
fluent answer to a question the user did not ask. Nothing errors and nothing is
logged.

Sample the hits and check by hand what fraction were genuinely the same
question, and report it with an interval. Note also that embedding similarity
does not track meaning where it matters most: @sec-embeddings showed antonyms
scoring as high as related words, and the sentence-level version of that is
measured above — a sentence and its negation at 0.982, the top of the list.
That is exactly the pair a cache must not conflate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your outputs changed overnight and nothing was deployed. Where do you look?

At the model identifier, and at whether it is pinned.

An unversioned alias points at whatever the provider currently serves, so a
model upgrade reaches production without a deploy, a diff or a test. It is a
dependency change that bypasses every gate you own, and it arrives on their
schedule.

The fix is structural: callers ask for an alias, the gateway resolves it to a
dated version, and migrations run behind an eval gate on a traffic slice. The
side benefit is reproducibility — a score against a floating alias is a score
for a model you can no longer name.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-gateway-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions below
recur in the two credible open sources this book uses throughout, plus the ones
this chapter's own measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the layer

**Q: What does a model gateway actually give you?**

Attribution and a choke point, and nothing else. It does not make a request
faster — that is @sec-serving — and it adds a hop. What it buys is that spend can
be attributed per team, keys rotated in one place, providers swapped without
editing callers, policy enforced once, and a deprecation notice turned into a
list of callers. Then say when *not* to build one: before the second team and
the second provider those problems do not exist, and the gateway is pure cost.

**Q: Can a gateway enforce a spending limit exactly?**

Not without capping output. Input tokens are countable before the request runs,
output tokens only after, and output is usually the dearer half. So enforcement
is either pessimistic — reserve `max_tokens` worth and reconcile down, which
under-serves — or optimistic, which can overshoot by about one request's worth of
output per concurrent caller. Setting `max_tokens` per virtual key turns an
unknown final cost into a reservable upper bound, and it is the step teams skip.

**Q: Your provider degrades and your gateway starts retrying. What happens?**

Potentially an outage you caused. Retries arrive exactly when the provider has
least capacity, so failures rise and retries rise with them. Name the three
controls: exponential backoff *with jitter*, because backoff alone
re-synchronises the fleet; a circuit breaker, so you stop paying latency to
rediscover an outage; and a retry budget as a fraction of traffic — Google's
clients stop retrying once retries pass 10% of their requests, on top of a
three-attempt per-request cap. Then add that only one layer should retry,
and that a 400 is not worth retrying at all.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: Your fallback provider kicked in overnight and nobody noticed. Good or bad?**

Bad, and the reliability part is the least of it. A fallback is a *different
model*: output format, tool-call syntax and refusal behaviour all differ, so a
parser tuned on the primary may reject the fallback's output, and quality
changed without an evaluation. Either the fallback path is on the same eval
suite as the primary, or the gateway fails closed with a clear error. Silently
serving an untested model is the option nobody chose and many ship.

**Q: How would you cut LLM spend 30% without a quality regression?**

Measure before choosing. Exact-match response caching first, where the key captures the relevant state
— tenant, permissions, data version — and repeated answers are acceptable; its
hit rate is a property of your traffic you can measure in
an afternoon. Then the prompt-side levers from @sec-serving, since on
prompt-heavy workloads — a system prompt plus retrieved context — input
dominates the bill even though output costs more per token. Only then routing — and say that routing is a claim needing
evidence: you need the cheap model's accuracy, the expensive one's, and a signal
that says in advance which requests need which. If the signal does not beat
random escalation at the same rate, routing is buying nothing.

**Q: Design the migration off a model being retired in 60 days.**

Enumerate the callers from the gateway's request log — the step that is
impossible without one. Point the alias at the new version for a small traffic
share, score both on the production eval suite (@sec-production-eval), and
promote on the evidence. Keep the old version pinned and available for
comparison until the deadline, and say plainly that an unversioned alias makes
every historical score unreproducible, which is why the pin comes first.

## Lab: a gateway that stops a runaway loop {#sec-gateway-lab}

The point of this lab is to watch a control actually fire. A budget nobody has
seen trigger is a configuration, not a control.

### Step 1 — put one proxy in front of one provider

Any gateway will do, including forty lines of your own. It needs three things:
it forwards requests, it records `(virtual key, model, input tokens, output
tokens)` per call, and it can refuse.

### Step 2 — give two callers separate virtual keys

Two keys, two notional teams, one real provider key behind them. Send traffic
through both and produce a per-key spend table. If you cannot produce that
table, nothing later in this lab is enforceable.

### Step 3 — set a budget you will actually hit

Small enough to trigger within a few minutes of ordinary traffic. Then run an
agent loop with no step cap — @sec-agent-anatomy's failure mode — against one of
the keys and watch the budget stop it. Record how much it spent *after* crossing
the limit, because that overshoot is what the asymmetry in @sec-gateway-budgets
costs you.

### Step 4 — cap output on one key, not the other

Set `max_tokens` on one virtual key and repeat step 3. The overshoot should
shrink to something predictable. Report both numbers; the difference is the
argument for capping output.

### Step 5 — add exact-match caching and measure the hit rate

Key on `(model version, prompt, parameters)` plus the tenant, the caller's
permissions and the version of the data the answer drew on — the list from
@sec-gateway-cache, not the prompt alone. Replay a realistic hour of traffic — real
if you have it, synthetic with repeated questions if you do not — and report the
hit rate and the saving. Send the same prompt through both virtual keys and
confirm they do not share an entry. Update one document a cached answer depended
on and confirm that entry stops being served. Then say, honestly, what share of
your real traffic you expect to repeat exactly.

### Step 6 — check the embedder before you trust a semantic cache

Before measuring any similarity threshold, embed two inputs that *must* differ
and confirm the model can tell them apart. This chapter's embedder could not:
every capitalised word collapsed to one vector. Five minutes, and it is the
difference between a cache and a random-answer generator.

### Step 7 — break failover on purpose

Point a fallback at a *different* model. Send twenty requests whose output you
parse — structured output from @sec-decoding is ideal — then force the primary to
fail and send the same twenty. Count how many the parser rejects.

### What to hand in

The per-key spend table; the overshoot with and without an output cap; the cache
hit rate, with the isolation and invalidation checks; your embedder sanity check; the parser failure count on the fallback
path; and one paragraph on whether your fallback should fail open (serve the
fallback's answer anyway) or closed (return an error), with the number that
justifies it.

## Exercises {#sec-gateway-exercises}

1. **The attribution question.** For a system you work on, answer without
   guessing: which team spent the most on LLM calls last month? Write down how
   long it took to find out, and what you would need for it to take a minute.

2. **Budget overshoot.** Compute, for a workload you know, how far a budget can
   be exceeded under optimistic admission: concurrent callers times the cost of
   `max_tokens` of output. Decide whether that number is tolerable, and cap
   output if it is not.

3. **The retry storm, on paper.** Take a service with a known request rate and a
   policy of at most three attempts per request. Compute the load a provider
   sees when half of all attempts start failing (assume each attempt fails
   independently), then when all of them fail. Recompute with a 10% retry
   budget and compare. Then add a second layer that also retries three times.

4. **Fallback equivalence.** Run one prompt you rely on against your primary and
   your fallback model. Diff the outputs — format, length, refusals, tool-call
   syntax — and decide whether your parser survives. Write the answer down before
   you need it at 3am.

5. **Cache hit rate, measured.** Instrument exact-match caching on real traffic
   for a day. Report the hit rate, the saving, and the share of misses that were
   *near*-misses. That last number is what a semantic cache would be tempted by.

6. **Audit your embedder.** Take whatever embedding model you would use for
   retrieval or caching and test it on pairs that must differ: a sentence and its
   negation, two dates, two order numbers, two proper nouns. Report the
   similarities. If any pair returns 1.000, stop and find out why.

7. **Routing, with a control.** Build a cascade on your own task: a small model,
   a large one, and an escalation signal. Report accuracy and cost at several
   escalation rates, and always report the random-escalation baseline alongside.
   If your signal does not beat random, say so.

8. **Pin audit.** List every model identifier your code sends. Mark which are
   dated pins and which are floating aliases. For each floating one, say what
   would happen — and how you would find out — if the provider moved it tonight.

## What to remember {#sec-gateway-summary}

- **A gateway buys attribution and a choke point, nothing else.** It does not
  make a request faster — that is @sec-serving — and it adds a hop whose
  availability becomes a ceiling on everyone's. Build it when the second team,
  the second provider or the first loop-capable agent arrives, and not before.

- **You cannot price a request before you run it.** Input tokens are countable
  at admission, output tokens only at completion, and output is usually dearer.
  So a budget is enforced pessimistically, or it overshoots by about one
  request's worth of output per concurrent caller — unless you cap `max_tokens`
  per key, which is the control most often left unset.

- **Retries turn a degradation into an outage.** Backoff *with jitter*, because
  plain backoff re-synchronises the fleet; a circuit breaker; and a retry budget
  as a fraction of traffic. Google runs a three-attempt per-request cap *and* a
  per-client rule that stops retrying once retries pass 10% of that client's
  requests — the first still allows nearly 3× load in the worst case, the
  second brings it to about 1.1×. Retry only retryable errors, and at one
  layer only.

- **A failover is a model swap, so it is an evaluation problem.** Different
  format, different tool-call syntax, different refusals; a parser tuned on the
  primary may reject the fallback. Either evaluate the fallback path on the same
  suite, or fail closed with a clear error. Silently serving an untested model is
  the option nobody chose and many ship.

- **Routing is a claim about a signal, not about an architecture.** Published
  cascades and learned routers report real savings [@chen2023frugalgpt;
  @ong2024routellm], but every one of those results depends on knowing which
  requests are hard. The most tempting signal — asking the model how sure it is
  — was measured in @sec-classification at **AUROC 0.667** against 0.843 for a
  proper probability. Always report the random-escalation baseline; if the
  policy does not beat it, the escalation *rate* is doing the work.

- **Exact-match caching is nearly free money once the key is right; semantic
  caching is a correctness decision.** Measured on fifteen labelled pairs, the
  most similar pair in the set was **a sentence and its negation at 0.982**,
  while a genuinely identical question scored **0.609**. The classes overlap
  so heavily that no single threshold separates them: the cut with the fewest
  errors is to cache nothing at all, missing all five genuine repeats.

- **Check the embedder before trusting the cache.** In this chapter's setup,
  `nomic-embed-text` under `ollama` 0.24.0 mapped every capitalised word to one
  constant token: *Monday*, *Cat*, *Ankara* and *XYZZY* all produced
  byte-identical vectors, and *Cat sat on the mat* equalled *Dog sat on the
  mat*. Lowercase text was fine. The same symptom is reported upstream and
  fixed in later `ollama` releases — and that fix changes the vectors too. A
  cache built on it would answer Sunday's question with Monday's answer at
  similarity 1.000 and log nothing. It surfaced only because a pair that had to
  score low scored highest.

- **Pin the version; an alias is a dependency that changes without a deploy.**
  A silent provider upgrade bypasses every gate you own, and it also makes every
  historical evaluation unreproducible, because the score belongs to a model you
  can no longer name.

- **Policy belongs at one choke point.** Redaction, audit, residency and
  retention must hold for every call, and five implementations guarantee drift.
  A policy you cannot enforce in one place is a policy you are hoping about.
